text.p: Western and developing countries face a weekend of soul-searching under intense political and economic pressure over how to vote on a censure motion against China next week at the U.N. Human Rights Commission.
At the heart of the moral dilemma for 53 member governments is how to balance their own domestic political and trade agenda with their conscience and commitment to basic freedoms.
A senior U.S. government official told Reuters on Thursday that China appeared to be using "economic and political threats" in its intense lobbying campaign to silence all U.N. scrutiny.
Denmark and the United States have put a brave face on the prospects for their resolution criticising China, saying they hoped the number of co-sponsors would rise from 15 to 30.

John Shattuck, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for Democracy, Human Rights and Labour, is flying to Geneva at the weekend to rally votes, while European foreign ministers will continue to "work the phones".

But with the European Union itself split and unable to co-sponsor the resolution due to French and German reluctance, many diplomats expect China to escape censure for the seventh year in a row when the main U.N. rights body votes on Tuesday.
They complain of being subjected to a fierce campaign by Beijing, alleging trade and other pressures are piling up.

Asian states are expected to close ranks around China, while European countries rally around Denmark. But about a dozen "swing" votes are up for grabs -- mainly developing countries -- including six new Commission members this year, diplomats said.
"We are under intense diplomatic pressure from China, with implicit commercial overtones," one delegate from a major developing country told Reuters.
"We are under political pressure from the other side as well," he added, referring to the Western bloc. "We don't expect to have our voting instructions until after the weekend."
The delegate, who asked not to be named, said his capital had to make a tough and politically-sensitive choice: "It is a real headache. We are caught between a rock and a hard place."

Noting that the Commission was expected to continue its tradition of adopting resolutions condemning alleged violations in countries including Burma, Cuba, Iran and Iraq, he asked: "Why should only China be different? No one else asks for a no-action motion."
"I personally think the no-action motion will be sustained," he added, echoing a European envoy who told Reuters that the West was "still a few votes short".
Last year, 27 states voted in favour of China's no-action motion, 20 voted against with six abstentions.
In its annual human rights report for 1996, the U.S. State Department said China had effectively silenced public dissent by jailing or exiling virtually every active dissident.
Ever since the 1989 crackdown in Tiananmen Square, Western countries have tried to get the U.N. body to at least debate allegations of executions and torture in China.
But concern over China has been heightened at the main rights forum this year due to the prospect of Hong Kong reverting to the mainland on June 30.
Human rights groups are concerned Hong Kong's 6.4 million people will enjoy fewer political and civil freedoms under the rule of Beijing, which has not signed major global rights pacts.

In any event, the showdown on Tuesday is expected to be dramatic, with Chinese delegation head Wu Jianmin in the hot seat. Western diplomats have speculated that his job as Chinese ambassador to the U.N. in Geneva is riding on the vote.
